title: Namespace-scoped API key collision during rotation allowed short-lived cross-org refreshes
creator: Aisha Banerjee
description: Summary: Several customers reported that after rotating API keys in Dedicated and Private deployments, some user sessions successfully refreshed and gained access to resources in a different organization for a short window. This manifested as authorization errors and unexpected dataset visibility for affected customers. Impact spans Hosted (edge caches), Dedicated pools with cross-region metadata replication, and Private (VPC) where admin rotations were performed.
root_cause: A mismatch between the authoritative key metadata master and opportunistic lookups used by the token refresh path. The refresh flow performs a fast lookup using a compact fingerprint optimization (used to accelerate auth checks at the edge). When customers re-used key prefixes during rotation, new keys shared the same compact fingerprint. Because replication of the full key -> org binding to read replicas and edge caches is eventual, there was a short window where the refresh endpoint resolved the fingerprint to the new key record without a validated org binding. The refresh logic relied on cache metadata for org scoping instead of validating against the canonical master, allowing a token refresh to be minted against the wrong org for ~30-120s until replication completed.
steps_to_repro: 1) In a cluster with replica-based metadata propagation (Dedicated/Private), create an API key for org A with prefix XY
2) Rotate the API key by issuing a new key for org B that intentionally reuses the same short prefix/fingerprint, and push the new key to master
3) Trigger a token refresh using a client holding the old session (old session still points to prefix XY)
4) Observe token refresh succeeding and new access scoped to org B while master->replica propagation is still in-flight
5) After propagation completes, subsequent refreshes behave correctly and the window closes
mitigation: Hotfix deployed: token refresh now performs a master-validated org binding check if the cache lookup returns a recently-rotated fingerprint (added 5s safety window). Deployed to Hosted edges and Dedicated control planes.
Emergency cache purge run for impacted customer clusters to reduce risk of further mismatches.
Customer notifications sent with recommended immediate rotation guidance and temporary advise to avoid key prefix reuse.
Temporary rate-limit on fingerprint-only lookups to force fallbacks to canonical lookup under high churn.
fix_plan: 1) Remove reliance on compact fingerprint as sole key for authorization decisions; include full key id + namespace in cache keys (backend change across runtime + gateway).
2) Version key metadata so refresh endpoint can detect stale/transitioning records and refuse refreshes until authoritative binding confirmed.
3) Strengthen cross-region replication ordering guarantees for key metadata (leadered replication for key bindings), add replication lag metrics and alerts.
4) Add e2e regression tests simulating rotation + replication lag across Hosted/Dedicated/Private modes.
5) Post-fix: migrate existing cached entries to new namespaced keys and invalidate ambiguous fingerprints.
rollout_plan: Canary: runtime-1.22 patch to 5% of Hosted edge fleet + 2 Dedicated pools with high customer-impact flag (3h observation window), disable fingerprint fast-path for canary instances.
Ramp: 25% after 6h with successful metrics, 100% in 48h if no regressions.
Private customers: provide a CR (control-plane) patch and an ops playbook for on-prem application to apply within 72h; coordinate with SEs for guided rollouts.
Post-deploy: 7-day increased observability on refresh success rate, unexpected org-scoped token issuance, and replication lag.
testing_notes: Unit: add assertion that cache keys include namespace and reject ambiguous fingerprint-only responses.
Integration: test directed replication lag by delaying replica apply and asserting refresh is blocked until master confirmation.
Load: ensure new master-validated path scales under peak refresh rates (baseline + 2x), add fallback guard to avoid introducing CPU amplification.
Security: run internal pen-test for auth path changes and include SRE review of invalidation windows.
